title: AES Encryption Parameters: Modes, Padding, and Filling in the IV
description: How to fill in the AES mode, padding, hex IV, and output format in this site's symmetric tool, and what the blank-IV, wrong-key, and hex/Base64 errors mean.
content:
Pick an algorithm and mode, enter a passphrase and key, then add a hexadecimal IV, and the symmetric encryption tool on this site completes one AES encryption. The parts that trip people up are the IV and the output format, so the sections below walk through each field against the tool's real implementation.

The six fields one encryption takes

From top to bottom the panel holds Algorithm, Mode, Output Format, Key, IV, and Plaintext / Ciphertext, then the Encrypt and Decrypt buttons. Algorithm offers only AES, DES, RC4, and Rabbit; Mode offers only CBC, ECB, CFB, OFB, and CTR; Output Format offers only Base64 and Hex. There are no authenticated modes such as GCM or CCM, and no key agreement or key storage: the tool only turns a piece of text into ciphertext with a passphrase, and back again.

The mode dropdown does not apply to every algorithm. The code writes the mode into the cipher configuration only when the algorithm is not RC4 or Rabbit, so with either of those selected the dropdown value is ignored. IV handling is not uniform either: RC4 ignores the IV completely, while Rabbit still reads the IV and uses it in the computation, so choosing Rabbit with a non-empty IV makes the output change with the IV.

The key is not the passphrase itself

What you type into Key is not used directly as an AES key. Line 77 hardcodes the salt as the hex string 636c6f766572746f6f6c73 (which happens to be ASCII "clovertools"), and lines 80 to 84 call CryptoJS.EvpKDF to derive a 32-byte key using MD5, 1 iteration, and keySize 256/32. A comment in the CryptoJS source says this function corresponds to OpenSSL's EVP_BytesToKey, which is not the same thing as PBKDF2.

Nothing in the derivation is random, so the same passphrase yields the same key every time: clover-secret derives 62d67a827882be3b6e846666ff79d05cd5aa8a9c24381c5b966fb20a562a5d9b. With that key and one IV, encrypting hello clover twice gives 334655f38007aef2a0f164bc8cadb40b both times; only a different IV changes it to 214efeff18a2071fa654b83f5c1bfd20.

RFC 8018 section 4.1 explains what a salt does: it lets one passphrase map to a large number of possible keys, so an attacker can only search passphrases for each salt separately. Section 4.2 cites the SP 800-132 recommendation that the iteration count be as large as users can tolerate, and at least 1000. This site's derivation chain uses 1 iteration and a fixed salt, so its job is to stretch a passphrase of any length into 32 bytes, not to slow down a passphrase-by-passphrase search.

Switching algorithms does not change the key length: DES takes only the first 8 bytes of the 32, Rabbit takes only the first 16, and RC4 uses all 32. DES ciphertext computed from the first 8 bytes is identical to ciphertext from the full derived key, and the same holds for Rabbit; RC4 with a 16-byte key, however, produces different ciphertext (add8585e17c1692a7d5300186a versus 6db1136d35162490db945dc60f).

How the five modes actually differ

The five dropdown entries correspond to several of the block cipher modes for confidentiality defined in NIST SP 800-38A. This site passes them to CryptoJS unchanged and requires an IV whenever the mode is not ECB. The differences show up plainly in errors and results:

Mode IV required here Actual behavior
CBC Required, 32 hex characters The IV feeds the first block; decrypt the same ciphertext with another IV and the first block comes out different
ECB Not required, and ignored if provided Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, fine for demos only
CFB Required, same branch as CBC Throws the same message when the IV is empty
OFB Required, same branch as CBC Throws the same message when the IV is empty
CTR Required, same branch as CBC Same as above, and under AES CryptoJS still pads in 16-byte blocks

ECB deserves a separate look. Encrypt a plaintext made of 32 abcd characters arranged as two blocks, and ECB returns two identical ciphertext blocks (both 9dbec8d37b6941e6365653d6915b6468), while the two CBC blocks differ (fe66930ca9a4b508c8f10883ecd8c748 and 257de9ee3bcf8ce56902c9e07f3981da). Any repeated 16-byte fragment in the plaintext survives as a repeated fragment in the ciphertext under ECB.

One more point: none of the dropdown entries is an authenticated mode. MDN's description of SubtleCrypto.encrypt recommends preferring authenticated encryption and notes that CBC and CTR provide no integrity check by default, so a tampered ciphertext is not detected; this site's output is just the ciphertext, with no authentication tag at all.

Padding: 5 characters still output 16 bytes

CryptoJS block ciphers use PKCS#7 padding by default, filling the plaintext up to a multiple of 16 bytes. Running the tool gives: plaintexts of 5 and 11 bytes both output 16 bytes of ciphertext, 16 bytes outputs 32, 17 bytes outputs 32, and 32 bytes outputs 48. A 16-byte plaintext becomes 32 bytes because PKCS#7 adds a whole extra block when the length already divides evenly.

CTR behaves the same: a 5-byte plaintext still outputs 16 bytes. CryptoJS's streaming modes go through the same block and padding logic, so don't expect switching to CTR to save those bytes.

Knowing this makes length a first-pass check. A 16-byte ciphertext is 32 hex characters or 24 Base64 characters (ending in ==); if the hex you paste is 30 or 33 characters long, a character was lost or added during the copy, and no change of key or IV will decrypt it correctly.

There is also an asymmetry: encryption does not trim the plaintext, so one trailing space changes the ciphertext completely (hello is 9133db62e0212f2eac8559b78161ba4a, hello plus a space is 4cda43142a1ee427278c33a7ea6a996d); decryption trims its input first, so newlines picked up when pasting ciphertext do not affect parsing.

IV: 32 hex characters, and blank throws an error

The IV field's placeholder says "Leave blank to auto-generate", but the code does not do that: in any mode other than ECB, an empty IV throws "This mode requires a hexadecimal IV." As it stands, leaving it blank does not generate one; you have to fill it in.

The format must be hexadecimal, and 32 characters is exactly 16 bytes. MDN's description of the iv parameter for AES-CBC says it must be 16 bytes, unpredictable, and preferably generated by a cryptographic random source, but it does not need to be secret and can be transmitted alongside the ciphertext. To generate one, run node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(16).toString('hex'))", and the output is 32 hex characters.

The tool does not validate the IV's length or characters. An IV like 00, one byte long, still encrypts, and decrypts back to hello clover with the same IV; decrypting the same ciphertext with a standard 16-byte IV yields fragments such as hdnok (a two-byte 0001 gives henok instead, which is just as unreadable). Entering non-hex content such as zz does not raise an error either, because Hex.parse turns zz into a single zero byte, equivalent to an all-zero IV: for plaintext of 15 bytes or less there is only one block, and the ciphertext is exactly the same as ECB with no IV; from 16 bytes on, padding produces at least a second block (32 bytes gives three), CBC chains the previous ciphertext block from the second block on, and the result diverges from ECB. A short or dirty IV does not fail on the spot; it just leaves the other side unable to decrypt even with the correct IV.

The IV does not need to be secret, but it must reach the other side together with the ciphertext. The output box holds only the ciphertext, with no IV, no mode, and no algorithm name, so when decrypting elsewhere you have to supply those missing pieces yourself.

Hex or Base64

When encrypting, the Output Format dropdown decides whether ciphertext is rendered as hex or base64; when decrypting, the dropdown plays no part, and the code tests the whole input with /^[0-9a-fA-F]+$/: a match is treated as hex, anything else as Base64. That is the trap: a ciphertext that is genuinely Base64 but happens to consist only of 0-9, a-f, and A-F will be read as hex.

Short ciphertexts collide easily. RC4-encrypting 0bh gives hex f5df5c and Base64 9d9c, and pasting 9d9c into the decrypt box parses it as hex and yields X! instead of 0bh. AES on short plaintext gives 24-character Base64 that ends in ==, which is essentially never misread, but that only shows the format decision rests on how the input looks, not on which format you selected earlier.

The safe habit is to stick to one format: encrypt as Hex and paste Hex to decrypt, encrypt as Base64 and paste Base64, with no conversions in between. Hexadecimal accepts either letter case, so ABCD is normalized to abcd; an odd number of hex characters is not rejected either, and abc parses as 1.5 bytes, but whatever such input decrypts to is meaningless.

What each common error means

Message Trigger What to do
"Please enter a key and content." The Key or content box is empty; encryption and decryption share this message Fill in both, then click again
"This mode requires a hexadecimal IV." Any mode other than ECB with an empty IV Enter 32 hex characters; only ECB may be left blank
"Decryption failed: Malformed UTF-8 data" The decrypted bytes are not valid UTF-8, usually a wrong key or IV Check the algorithm, mode, key, and IV
"Decryption result is empty. Check the key, IV, or mode." An empty string was decrypted, and the code throws deliberately As above, and check whether the ciphertext was truncated or misread

Decrypting the same AES-CBC ciphertext with wrong passphrases gave "Decryption result is empty" 193 times out of 200 and Malformed UTF-8 data 7 times. Both messages point at the same thing: the key is wrong. The tool cannot say "wrong passphrase" directly, because CBC has no check bits, and a wrong key only produces garbage.

"Decryption result is empty" has another source: the ciphertext format was misjudged, or its length is not a multiple of 16 bytes. The 9d9c case above decrypts to content that is simply wrong; pasting half a ciphertext gives an empty result or garbled text. Check the length first, then the IV, and finally switch back to the algorithm and mode used for encryption.

Boundaries and limits

  • Derivation is deterministic: fixed salt, 1 iteration, MD5, so the same passphrase always gives the same key, and the same plaintext with the same IV reproduces the same ciphertext. It offers no random salt and no iteration cost.
  • The IV is entered by hand: the tool neither generates it nor validates its length or characters, so a 1-byte IV or one containing invalid characters still encrypts, at the cost of nobody being able to decrypt it.
  • No authentication: the output is only ciphertext, with no tag of any kind; MDN notes that CBC and CTR provide no integrity check by default, so a modified ciphertext is not reported as tampering.
  • No metadata in the output: salt, IV, mode, and algorithm name are all absent from the result. With openssl, supplying the derived key via -K and the same IV decrypts hello clover, but handing over the passphrase with -pass reports bad magic number, because that path expects the input to carry its own salt header.
  • Algorithm and key length do not match up: DES consumes only 8 bytes and Rabbit only 16, while all four algorithms share one derivation chain, so old ciphertext cannot be decrypted across a switch of algorithm.
  • Limited purpose: the page script only reads and writes the input boxes in the browser, with no upload step; but it does no file encryption and no key management, and it is not suitable for protecting genuinely sensitive data.

If the need is not "turn a piece of text back into the original", several tools here fit better: to check only whether content was modified, use hashing; to put ciphertext into a URL or JSON, confirm the format first with Base64 encoding; to hand a key to someone instead of sharing a passphrase, use RSA encryption; to store login passphrases, use a slow hash such as bcrypt rather than reversible encryption.

Fill it in, step by step

  1. Choose AES as the algorithm and CBC as the mode to start. ECB can leave the IV blank, but repeated plaintext blocks leave repeated ciphertext blocks, so it is only for demos.
  2. Type the passphrase into Key; clicking "Sample" fills in clover-secret, which makes it easy to match the numbers above.
  3. Put 32 hex characters in IV, generated with the randomBytes command above, and do not leave it blank.
  4. Set Output Format to Hex, paste the plaintext, click Encrypt, and note down the ciphertext.
  5. To decrypt, set Algorithm, Mode, Key, and IV back to the encryption values, paste the same ciphertext, and click Decrypt.

To confirm the mode is not left on the wrong setting, encrypt the same plaintext once under each of two IVs: CBC ciphertext changes with the IV, while ECB is completely unaffected by it. If the two results are identical, the mode is still on ECB.

faqs.q: Does leaving the IV blank generate one automatically?
faqs.a: No. The placeholder says "Leave blank to auto-generate", but any mode other than ECB checks for an empty IV and throws "This mode requires a hexadecimal IV." straight away. For now you must enter 32 hex characters yourself; only ECB needs no IV, and an IV entered there is ignored.

faqs.q: Why is the result exactly the same when I encrypt with the same passphrase twice?
faqs.a: Derivation uses the fixed salt 636c6f766572746f6f6c73, MD5, and 1 iteration, with nothing random. As long as the key, mode, IV, and plaintext all stay the same, the ciphertext is exactly the same; to get something different each time, use a different IV on every run in a non-ECB mode.

faqs.q: What does "Malformed UTF-8 data" mean when decrypting?
faqs.a: The decrypted bytes are not valid UTF-8 text. Trying 200 wrong passphrases against the same AES-CBC ciphertext gave "Decryption result is empty" 193 times and this error 7 times. Both point to the same thing: the algorithm, mode, key, or IV does not match the ones used for encryption.

faqs.q: Why does a Base64 ciphertext fail to decrypt?
faqs.a: Decryption decides the format with /^[0-9a-fA-F]+$/, so Base64 made up only of hex characters is treated as hex. The Base64 for RC4-encrypting 0bh is 9d9c, which is read as hex and decrypts to X! instead of 0bh. Sticking to one format avoids it: choose Hex to encrypt, and always paste Hex.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-38A：Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation

focus: The passphrase is first derived into a 32-byte key, then encrypted with the mode and IV; any mode other than ECB requires you to enter a 32-character hex IV yourself.
notice: Derivation and encryption both run locally in your browser, so content is never uploaded; the fixed salt and 1 iteration are only suitable for demos and format checks, so do not hand real sensitive data to it.
